_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Brunei covering early Hindu-Buddhist settlements, Srivijaya/Majapahit influence, conversion to Islam (14th century), Brunei Sultanate golden age (15th-16th century, controlled most of Borneo and Philippines), European contact (Magellan, Spanish, Portuguese), cession of Sarawak to James Brooke (1841), British residency, Japanese occupation, oil discovery, independence 1984, and Hassanal Bolkiah's modern Brunei.

country_profile.currency: Brunei dollar (BND, pegged to Singapore dollar)

religion.note: Official state ideology: Melayu Islam Beraja (MIB — Malay Islamic Monarchy); Sharia Penal Code implemented 2014/2019

ethnic_groups.name: Malay
ethnic_groups.notes: Dominant; Brunei Malay (Melayu Brunei); seven constituent groups recognised in constitution: Belait, Bisaya, Brunei, Dusun, Kedayan, Murut, Tutong

ethnic_groups.name: Chinese
ethnic_groups.notes: Hokkien, Hakka, Cantonese; long-standing trading community; some are permanent residents not citizens; commercial sector

ethnic_groups.name: Indigenous (Iban, Dusun, Murut, etc.)
ethnic_groups.notes: Iban inland; Dusun and Murut in Temburong; Penan semi-nomadic; Bisaya; some still practice traditional religions

ethnic_groups.name: Indian/South Asian
ethnic_groups.notes: Tamil, Punjabi; professional and labour sectors

ethnic_groups.name: Other (expat workers)
ethnic_groups.notes: Large foreign workforce: Filipino, Indonesian, Thai, Bangladeshi; oil/gas and domestic workers

country_profile.notes_unique: One of the wealthiest nations; no personal income tax; free education and healthcare; Sultan's palace (Istana Nurul Iman) is world's largest residential palace; two non-contiguous parts separated by Sarawak

current_leader.name: Hassanal Bolkiah
current_leader.title: Sultan and Yang di-Pertuan
current_leader.notes: 29th Sultan of Brunei; one of world's longest-reigning monarchs (57+ years); also PM, Defence and Finance Minister; one of world's wealthiest individuals; led to independence from UK 1984

crown_prince.name: Al-Muhtadee Billah
crown_prince.title: Crown Prince and Senior Minister
crown_prince.notes: Heir apparent; plays increasing governmental role

former_sultans.name: Omar Ali Saifuddien III
former_sultans.notes: 'Architect of Modern Brunei'; built Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque; rejected joining Malaysia 1963; abdicated in favour of son but remained influential until death 1986

former_sultans.name: Sultan Muhammad Shah (Awang Alak Betatar)
former_sultans.notes: First Muslim sultan; converted from Hindu-Buddhist; established Islamic dynasty; Chinese records mention Brunei tribute

910.name: Early Settlements and Proto-Bruneian Cultures
910.description: Prehistoric human habitation along the Borneo coast, early Austronesian migrations, and the emergence of maritime trade communities that would form the cultural substrate of later Bruneian polities.

sub_clusters.name: Prehistoric Borneo and Austronesian Migrations
sub_clusters.description: Archaeological evidence of early settlement in northern Borneo, cave sites, and the arrival of Austronesian-speaking peoples who brought rice cultivation and seafaring traditions.

sub_clusters.name: Early Maritime Trade Contacts
sub_clusters.description: Initial contacts with Indian and Chinese traders, the development of coastal trading settlements, and the gradual integration into wider Southeast Asian maritime exchange networks.

920.name: Po-ni Kingdom and Indianized Polity
920.description: The emergence of Po-ni (Boni) as recorded in Chinese dynastic histories, its tributary missions to China, Hindu-Buddhist cultural influences, and the development of a maritime trading state on the Borneo coast.

sub_clusters.name: Po-ni in Chinese Records
sub_clusters.description: The first recorded Chinese embassy from Po-ni to the Liang dynasty in 518 AD, subsequent tribute missions, and the kingdom's role in maritime trade between China and the Malay world.
key_events: First recorded embassy from Po-ni to China's Liang dynasty (518 AD)
Po-ni sends tribute to the Song dynasty, indicating continued diplomatic ties (977 AD)

sub_clusters.name: Hindu-Buddhist Influences and Srivijayan Connections
sub_clusters.description: The diffusion of Hindu-Buddhist religious practices, possible Srivijayan suzerainty, the kingdom's cultural and economic ties with Javanese and Malay polities, and the gradual transition toward Islam.

930.name: Sultanate of Brunei Golden Age
930.description: The conversion to Islam and founding of the Sultanate, Brunei's rise as a major maritime power controlling much of northern Borneo, the Philippines trade, and its zenith under Sultan Bolkiah.

sub_clusters.name: Conversion to Islam and Sultanate Founding
sub_clusters.description: The legendary conversion of Awang Alak Betatar as Sultan Muhammad Shah, the establishment of the Islamic sultanate, Chinese Ming dynasty relations, and the growth of Brunei as a regional center.
key_events: Conversion to Islam and establishment of the Sultanate of Brunei (c. 1368)
Sultan Abdul Majid Hassan (Ma-ha-mo-sha) visits the Ming court and dies in Nanjing (1408)

sub_clusters.name: Zenith Under Sultan Bolkiah
sub_clusters.description: The reign of Sultan Bolkiah, the 'Singing Captain', Brunei's territorial expansion across northern Borneo and into the Sulu Archipelago and Manila, and the height of Bruneian maritime commerce.
key_events: Sultan Bolkiah extends Bruneian control over Manila and the Sulu Archipelago (c. 1500)

sub_clusters.name: Spanish Encounters and Contestation
sub_clusters.description: Magellan's expedition and contact with Brunei, the Castile War of 1578 when Spain attacked Brunei, and the beginning of European encroachment in Bruneian waters.
key_events: Antonio Pigafetta describes the grandeur of the Brunei court during Magellan's voyage (1521)
Spain attacks and briefly occupies Kota Batu in the Castile War (1578)

940.name: Decline and Territorial Contraction
940.description: Internal succession crises, civil wars, piracy, the loss of territories to the Sulu Sultanate, and the gradual erosion of Bruneian power as European colonial interests encroached on Borneo.

sub_clusters.name: Civil Wars and Succession Crises
sub_clusters.description: Recurring dynastic disputes, the weakening of central authority, the loss of Manila to Spain, and the fragmentation of Bruneian control over outlying territories.

sub_clusters.name: Piracy and Sulu Rivalry
sub_clusters.description: The rise of Sulu as a rival power, the loss of Bruneian territories in Sabah and the southern Philippines, widespread piracy in Bruneian waters, and the sultanate's declining revenues.

940.name: Brooke Dynasty and British Intervention
940.description: James Brooke's acquisition of Sarawak, the progressive cession of Bruneian territories to the Brooke Rajahs and the British North Borneo Company, and the near-extinction of the sultanate.

sub_clusters.name: James Brooke and Sarawak Cession
sub_clusters.description: James Brooke's intervention in the Sarawak rebellion, his appointment as Rajah of Sarawak, progressive Bruneian territorial losses, and the Treaty of Protection with Britain in 1888.
key_events: Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien II cedes Sarawak to James Brooke (1841)
Brunei becomes a British Protected State under the Treaty of Protection (1888)

sub_clusters.name: Near-Extinction and British Residency
sub_clusters.description: Continued territorial losses to Sarawak, the cession of the Limbang district in 1890, and the establishment of a British Residency system in 1906 that effectively removed the sultan's governing authority.

950.name: British Residency and Japanese Occupation
950.description: British colonial administration through the Residency system, the discovery of oil at Seria in 1929, the devastating Japanese occupation during World War II, and Allied liberation.

sub_clusters.name: Oil Discovery and Colonial Development
sub_clusters.description: The British Resident's administration, the discovery of oil at Seria in 1929, the transformation of Brunei's economy, and the modernization of infrastructure.
key_events: Discovery of the Seria oil field transforms Brunei's economic future (1929)

sub_clusters.name: Japanese Occupation
sub_clusters.description: The Japanese invasion and occupation of Brunei during World War II, exploitation of oil resources, the suffering of the civilian population, and the Australian-led liberation in June 1945.
key_events: Australian forces liberate Brunei in Operation Oboe Six (June 1945)

950.name: Path to Independence
950.description: Post-war reconstruction, Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III's modernization programs, the 1962 revolt, the decision not to join Malaysia, and the achievement of full independence from Britain.

sub_clusters.name: Post-War Reconstruction and Modernization
sub_clusters.description: The restoration of British protection, Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III's modernization drive, the 1959 constitution, and growing nationalist sentiments.

sub_clusters.name: Brunei Revolt and Road to Sovereignty
sub_clusters.description: The 1962 Brunei Revolt led by A.M. Azahari, the declaration of emergency, Brunei's decision to remain outside the Federation of Malaysia, and the achievement of full independence on 1 January 1984.
key_events: Brunei Revolt against proposed merger with Malaysia suppressed with British help (December 1962)
Brunei achieves full independence from the United Kingdom (1 January 1984)

960.name: Modern Brunei Darussalam
960.description: Independent Brunei under the Malay Islamic Monarchy philosophy, the management of oil and gas wealth, the diversification agenda, Sharia law implementation, and Brunei's role in ASEAN.

sub_clusters.name: Oil Wealth and Melayu Islam Beraja
sub_clusters.description: The consolidation of Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah's absolute monarchy, the Melayu Islam Beraja national philosophy, the development of a welfare state funded by oil and gas revenues, and the 1998 constitutional crisis involving Prince Jefri.
key_events: Brunei joins ASEAN as its sixth member (1984)
Amedeo Development Corporation scandal involving Prince Jefri Bolkiah (1998)

sub_clusters.name: Sharia Implementation and Diversification
sub_clusters.description: The phased implementation of Sharia Penal Code from 2014, international controversy over hudud punishments, Brunei Vision 2035 economic diversification efforts, and the country's role in ASEAN and regional diplomacy.
key_events: Brunei implements Sharia Penal Code Order provoking international criticism (2014–2019)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
